title: Restrain and Sustain 2026
author: Adam Boxer
summary: Adam Boxer uses a composite scenario of a school CPD calendar to name two common mistakes in school improvement. The first is doing too much, as when a leadership team schedules six sessions on six topics, which no staff can absorb. The second is moving on too quickly, treating a single training session as if it had embedded a practice. His remedy is the pair of verbs in the title: restrain the urge to add initiatives, and sustain attention on one priority by visiting classrooms and following up. He supports the first point with his own school's record of only four whole-school Teaching and Learning priorities in seven years. The piece ends by redefining school improvement as changed classrooms rather than topics covered or policy pages written.
points: Boxer argues that planning a full year of CPD topics in advance guarantees overload, because teachers are already busy.
He updates his earlier advice to subtract something when adding something, preferring the broader idea of restraint for optimistic leaders.
Sustaining focus means getting into classrooms after a session to check take-up, support and the effectiveness of delivery.
Umbrella terms such as adaptive teaching or oracy hide many strategies, so leaders should pick one concrete behaviour they want to see in every lesson.
Success is measured by changed classroom practice, not by the number of CPD topics covered or pages in a policy.
quotes: Teachers, as we all know, are extremely busy people, and taking on anything new is going to be a tall order, let alone asking them to take on six things in any given year.
I often tell visitors to The Totteridge Academy that across the 7 years I’ve been lucky enough to work there, the leadership team have only had 4 whole-school Teaching and Learning priorities.
It seems to me that when it comes to professional development in schools, less is more.
Don’t lose the energy and the passion, but narrow it down to a smaller set of priorities. Hold back.

Every teacher is now doing adaptive teaching, and we can move on to the next thing. Experience tells us that this is categorically not the case, and even tweaks and changes that appear simple and easy take a long time to embed and refine.
Instead, they should look at the list of things they want to introduce, then rank the items by priority, and start by focusing on just one.
In short, leaders should sustain their focus on the first thing, rather than move on to the second thing.
Leading professional development is about changing real classrooms, and if you don’t restrain your enthusiasm and sustain your attention, those classrooms will look no different.
